resources.title: Prepare for a first legal consultation
resources.summary: A practical question list, without sharing private details online.

sections.title: Write a short timeline
sections.text: For your own records, note what happened, where it happened and the approximate date. Mark anything you are unsure about. Bring questions rather than trying to decide the legal outcome yourself.

sections.title: Ask who will handle the matter
sections.text: Ask which lawyer would be responsible for your case, who would communicate with you and how you can reach the team. Discuss relevant experience and conflicts before sending documents.

sections.title: Bring a focused question list
sections.text: Ask about the possible process, what information is needed, the expected communication schedule and the written fee agreement. Keep original records and request a secure way to share copies.

sections.title: Leave with a clear next step
sections.text: Confirm whether the lawyer has agreed to represent you, what you need to do next and who will track any time limits. A website inquiry by itself does not establish representation.

resources.title: Questions to ask about fees and costs
resources.summary: Understand the written agreement before deciding to hire a lawyer.

sections.title: Separate fees from expenses
sections.text: A contingency arrangement generally ties attorney fees to a recovery. Case expenses are a separate question. Ask who advances costs and who is responsible if there is no recovery.

sections.title: Ask for the agreement in writing
sections.text: Read how the fee is calculated, what expenses can be deducted and what happens if another lawyer joins the case. Ask about any term you do not understand before signing.

sections.title: Do not rely on a slogan
sections.text: A short advertisement cannot describe every term in an agreement. Request an explanation of the actual fee and cost arrangement that would apply to your matter.

resources.title: A private record organizer
resources.summary: An original checklist you can use offline to prepare questions.

sections.title: Create a folder you control
sections.text: Keep copies of correspondence, incident reference numbers and documents you already have. Use a secure personal location. This checklist does not ask you to upload any record.

sections.title: Keep a contact log
sections.text: For each conversation, record the date, the person's name, their organization and the next step discussed. Distinguish exact notes from your later recollection.

sections.title: Prepare a missing-information list
sections.text: List records you may want to ask a lawyer about. Do not obtain someone else's private records or access accounts without permission. Ask the lawyer how relevant material should be preserved.

sections.title: Bring questions, not medical uploads
sections.text: Before sharing health, insurance or identity documents, confirm who will receive them and ask for a secure channel. Avoid putting private information into website search boxes or general contact messages.

resources.title: Why a filing deadline needs individual review
resources.summary: Different claims and facts can have different timing rules.

sections.title: There is no single deadline for every injury
sections.text: Florida's limitations statute sets different periods for different types of actions. Other provisions, notice requirements and facts may affect a particular matter. This page does not calculate a deadline.

sections.title: Do not wait for an online answer
sections.text: Ask a licensed Florida lawyer to review the incident date, claim type and parties involved promptly. A contact form, saved checklist or unanswered message does not pause a legal time limit.

sections.title: What to ask
sections.text: Ask which timing rules may apply, what facts the lawyer needs to check and who is responsible for taking the next action. Confirm any advice directly with the lawyer rather than treating this general guide as an assessment.

resources.title: How to evaluate a lawyer before hiring
resources.summary: Check credentials, fit, communication and the proposed agreement.

sections.title: Verify the person
sections.text: Use The Florida Bar's member directory to check the lawyer's public profile. Compare the name and contact information with the person you are speaking to. A directory listing is a starting point, not a promise about the outcome of a case.

sections.title: Discuss fit and communication
sections.text: Ask about work relevant to your situation, who would be responsible and how updates will be provided. Tell the lawyer your priorities and ask how decisions are made.

sections.title: Compare the proposed agreement
sections.text: Understand the scope of representation, fees and expenses before hiring. Keep a copy of the written agreement. If you do not understand a term, ask for an explanation.

resources.title: A plain-language consultation process
resources.summary: Understand the difference between an inquiry, review and representation.

sections.title: 1. Make an initial inquiry
sections.text: A verified advertiser can explain its intake process and the information it needs. Ask for the name of the recipient and a secure channel before sending sensitive material.

sections.title: 2. Discuss whether the lawyer can help
sections.text: The lawyer may need to review the facts, check conflicts and explain the possible scope of services. An initial conversation does not guarantee that the lawyer will accept the matter.

sections.title: 3. Review a written agreement
sections.text: If both sides decide to proceed, discuss the representation and the fee and cost terms. Confirm when the lawyer's responsibilities begin and what the next step will be.
